raw.abstractText:
Background

Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (AATD) caused by the PI*ZZ genotype (Glu342Lys) is characterized by hepatic accumulation of misfolded AAT-Z protein and reduced circulating AAT levels, leading to progressive liver disease and pulmonary emphysema. Gene correction therapy represents a potentially curative approach by directly correcting the underlying genetic defect. We report the first clinical case with direct assessment of hepatic gene correction by liver biopsy following in vivo base editing in a patient with AATD.

Methods/case presentation

We report the case of a 66-year-old male patient with PI*ZZ AATD who underwent gene correction therapy within the YOLT-202 phase I/Ia clinical trial (clinical trial.gov ID NCT07193615). Ten weeks after treatment a liver biopsy was performed to assess hepatic histology in the context of pre-existing F2 fibrosis identified by elastography before treatment. Liver tissue was analyzed for correction of the Pi*ZZ variant using Sanger and Illumina sequencing, including assessment of bystander and off-target editing. Serum levels and biological activity of AAT were assessed longitudinally using an elastase inhibition assay.

Results

Liver biopsy showed no evidence of hepatic inflammation and demonstrated correction of the PI*ZZ variant in 54% of alleles by Sanger and 57% by Illumina sequencing without detectable off-target signals. Following a transient post-treatment increase in transaminases, liver enzymes returned to baseline. Monthly measurements demonstrated sustained circulating AAT levels with preserved biological activity, as assessed by elastase inhibition, throughout follow-up.

Conclusions

In vivo base editing achieved substantial and precise hepatic correction of the pathogenic SERPINA1 PI*ZZ variant, without concerning histological findings or detectable bystander or off-target editing. Sustained biologically active AAT levels support feasibility and potential of this approach for the treatment of AATD.

raw.abstractText:
Background

 Fibrotic liver is one of the serious pathophysiological consequences of chronic injury to the liver, may progress toward serious complications including cirrhosis and hepatic carcinoma.

Objectives

Panax notoginseng is used for both therapeutic and prophylactic purposes in TCM; it is a source of Dencichine, an active substance that has been proven to exhibit antifibrotic properties in hepatic fibrosis. The present study investigated how Dencichine treatment ameliorates liver fibrosis using an animal model and a cellular fibrosis model.

Methods

Randomly assigned, male C57BL/6J mice received 10% CCl4 for 15 consecutive weeks to induce hepatic fibrosis. Treatment with Dencichine was initiated from 7th week onward. To simulate in-vitro the presence of a fibrotic microenvironment, LX-2 cells were treated with PDGF-BB at a concentration of 20 ng/mL and incubated from one up to four days and then treated by various doses of Dencichine. Liver function was evaluated by measuring alanine aminotransferase (ALT), AST, HA and LN. Histopathology was evaluated by haematoxylin/eosin (HE), Masson's trichrome and Sirius red stains. Quantitative real-time PCR and western blot analyses were used to evaluate mRNA and protein expression levels, respectively. Wound-healing assays and transwell chamber experiments were used to assess cell migration; EdU proliferation detection and flow cytometry were performed to measure cell proliferation and cell cycle, respectively.

Results

 The most important results are a considerable reduction of serum concentrations of AST and ALT, HA and laminin in CCl4-treated mice decreased liver injury and ECM deposition. Furthermore, this compound downregulated the expression of cyclin D1 and cyclin E1 and blocked the activation of PI3K and AKT kinases in fibrotic liver cells.

Conclusion

These results indicate that Dencichine may slow the development of liver fibrosis by interfering with the PI3K-AKT signaling cascade, demonstrating significant anti-scarring properties.

raw.abstractText:
Background

Tibial transverse osteotomy (TTO) is a promising but limited surgical option for diabetic foot (DF). Berberine, a natural compound from Coptis chinensis, exhibits anti-inflammatory and pro-angiogenic effects relevant to metabolic diseases.

Objectives

This study aimed to evaluate whether adjunctive berberine enhances the therapeutic outcomes of TTO in DF patients and to explore its potential association with the platelet-derived growth factor-B (PDGF-B)/PDGF receptor-β (PDGFRβ) signaling pathway.

Methods

This was a prospective, single-center, randomized, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, blinded trial. Of 200 screened DF patients, 96 eligible participants (Wagner grade 2-4) scheduled for TTO were randomized 1:1 to receive either TTO plus local berberine injections (n=48) or TTO plus local saline placebo (n=48). An additional non-randomized diabetic reference group (n=10) and healthy control group (n=10) were included for exploratory cellular studies only. The primary outcome was the total effective rate of ulcer healing at 3 months. Secondary outcomes included changes in Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI), ulcer area, Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) pain score and serum inflammatory markers (hs-CRP, IL-6). Exploratory outcomes comprised serum VEGF, bFGF and PDGF-B levels, as well as fibroblast apoptosis in wound tissue.

Results

All 96 randomized participants completed the 3-month follow-up, with no dropouts. The berberine group demonstrated a significantly higher total effective rate than the surgery-alone group (87.5% vs. 68.8%; risk difference, 18.7%; 95% CI, 1.2% to 36.2%; P < 0.05). At 3 months, the berberine group also showed greater improvements in ABI (mean difference, 0.13; 95% CI, 0.08 to 0.18; P < 0.01) and ulcer healing rate (mean difference, 16.7%; 95% CI, 9.5% to 23.9%; P < 0.01), along with more significant reductions in hs-CRP and IL-6. Berberine treatment was associated with reduced fibroblast apoptosis in wound tissue (mean difference, -1.10%; 95% CI, -1.56% to -0.64%; P = 0.001) and lower protein expression of PDGF-B and PDGFRβ. No severe adverse events related to berberine injections were reported.

Conclusion

In DF patients undergoing TTO, adjunctive local berberine therapy significantly improves the total effective rate and promotes ulcer healing, with benefits associated with reduced inflammation and fibroblast apoptosis and downregulation of the PDGF-B/PDGFRβ pathway. These findings are correlative and require further mechanistic validation. Larger multi-center trials are needed to confirm efficacy and safety.

raw.abstractText: Understanding cellular diversity within a tissue is essential to elucidate how distinct cell populations cooperate to maintain homeostasis, regenerate, and respond to aging or disease. Unlike bulk methods that measure averaged gene expression, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables high-resolution profiling of the transcriptomes of individual cells, providing a powerful tool for analyzing cellular heterogeneity. However, its application in skeletal muscle remains limited to the mononucleated cellular fraction, as standard single-cell approaches cannot efficiently capture muscle fibers due to their large and multinucleated nature. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq), which profiles individual nuclei rather than intact cells, offers a more suitable and technically robust approach, enabling comprehensive characterization of the transcriptional landscape across the entire tissue. In this chapter, we present a workflow for the bioinformatic analysis of snRNA-seq data generated from mouse skeletal muscle using the 10x Genomics Chromium platform. The chapter focuses on computational processing using R software and the Seurat package, including quality control, normalization, dimensionality reduction, clustering, and cell-type annotation. By applying this pipeline, researchers can identify distinct muscle-resident cell populations and explore the complexity of skeletal muscle. The described framework also illustrates how to perform downstream analyses such as differential gene expression and cell-cell communication analysis.

raw.abstractText: The molecular identification of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) from root tissues can often be limited by the co-extraction of polysaccharides, phenolic compounds, and other PCR inhibitors, particularly in woody or highly lignified roots, where cell lysis is also often difficult. Although commercial extraction kits offer standardized workflows and reduce the handling of harmful reagents, the manufacturer's protocols are insufficient for root samples with high levels of secondary metabolites. This protocol describes the optimization of DNA extraction from coffee (Coffea arabica L.) roots colonized by AMF, based on the use of the commercial ZymoBIOMICS™ Quick-DNA fecal/soil Microbe Kit, designed for the rapid and simple isolation of microbial DNA and host cells from fecal and soil samples, incorporating a pre-maceration and pre-digestion step with proteinase K and β-mercaptoethanol. This modification significantly improves yield, DNA integrity, and PCR amplification of Glomeromycota-specific ribosomal markers (SSU/18S).

raw.abstractText: Δ<sup>9</sup>-Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) is the principal psychoactive cannabinoid in cannabis. Following consumption, it is metabolized in the liver to 11-hydroxy-Δ<sup>9</sup>-tetrahydrocannabinol, and subsequently to 11-nor-9-carboxy-Δ<sup>9</sup>-tetrahydrocannabinol, which are excreted in urine. The presence of THC and its metabolites in urine can serve as indicators of recent or past cannabis use. Here, a routine method for the simultaneous quantification of these three compounds is presented, using tandem enzymatic-alkaline hydrolysis, solid-phase extraction, and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS). The procedure is optimized for operational efficiency and analytical sensitivity and is routinely applied to urine samples submitted for cannabinoid testing in clinical and forensic toxicology.

raw.abstractText: Tryptamines constitute a class of organic compounds structurally derived from tryptamine, a natural alkaloid found in plants, fungi, and the human body. This group encompasses biologically significant molecules such as serotonin and melatonin, as well as psychoactive compounds like DMT and psilocybin. Tryptamines are typically classified into simple tryptamines and ergolines, with further subclassifications based on structural modifications on the indole ring system. Their primary mechanism of action involves modulation of serotonergic receptors, especially the 5-HT2A, often resulting in psychedelic effects. While some tryptamines are naturally occurring, others are synthetically produced and increasingly encountered as new psychoactive substances. The study presents a rapid and robust LC-MS/MS method for the simultaneous detection and quantification of 37 tryptamines in human urine and plasma. The method employs a ThermoFisher UHPLC-LC-MS/MS system using a Hypersil GOLD C18 column and gradient elution, with MS^n acquisition in positive ESI mode. Analytical validation demonstrated high selectivity, sensitivity, and reproducibility. Sample preparation was performed through a combination of liquid-liquid and protein precipitation extraction procedures. The method successfully identified tryptamines using product ion spectra compared to a reference spectral library, with detection limits, recovery, and matrix effects systematically evaluated. This analytical approach provides a reliable tool for forensic and clinical toxicology, particularly in the context of the increasing interest in tryptamines for both recreational and therapeutic purposes.

raw.abstractText: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) represent the first line of host immune defense against a broad spectrum of microorganisms. Whether naturally occurring or synthetically designed, these small peptides can potently inhibit microbial growth and remain stable under diverse conditions. Most AMPs act by directly disrupting fungal or bacterial membranes. In this study, we identified a glycine-rich peptide with strong antifungal activity against Botrytis cinerea. We further investigated its mode of action (MOA) and demonstrated its preventive antifungal activity in plants. Our work focuses primarily on the in vitro characterization of AMP features in the context of plant-Botrytis interactions.

raw.abstractText: Virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) is a powerful reverse genetics tool that enables the transient knockdown of gene expression in plants by exploiting their natural antiviral defense mechanisms. This chapter presents a detailed protocol for applying a Cowpea severe mosaic virus (CPSMV)-based VIGS system to study gene function in soybean (Glycine max), with a focus on symbiotic root nodulation. VIGS allows systemic silencing of target genes, making it especially valuable to study pathways involving systemic signaling. The protocol includes Agrobacterium-mediated propagation of CPSMV variants in Nicotiana benthamiana, followed by mechanical inoculation of soybean plants and nodulation analysis. Detailed steps for vector construction, viral amplification, plant infection, and downstream molecular and phenotypic analyses are provided. This protocol is reproducible, accessible, and suitable for functional genomics studies in soybean, particularly for genes involved in nodulation but also in other developmental or stress-related processes.

raw.abstractText: Oligopeptide-modified poly(β-amino ester)s (OM-pBAEs) are polymer-based delivery systems that enable the encapsulation and intracellular transport of nucleic acids, including messenger RNA (mRNA) and mixtures of mRNA with DNA. OM-pBAEs form cationic nanoparticles (NPs) through electrostatic interactions with nucleic acids, protecting them from degradation and enhancing cellular uptake. Terminal oligopeptides composed of lysine, arginine, or histidine enhance polyplex stability, nucleic acid binding, and endosomal escape. This chapter describes a protocol for preparing OM-pBAE nanoparticles, including polymer synthesis, peptide modification, controlled mixing with nucleic acids to form polyplexes, precipitation in RNase-free water, stabilization with excipients, and optional freeze-drying for long-term storage. Nanoparticle formation occurs at a constant temperature of 25°C, with incubation to ensure reproducible self-assembly. Nanoparticles are characterized by using dynamic light scattering (DLS) to determine particle size, polydispersity, and surface charge, while nucleic acid encapsulation efficiency is assessed to evaluate loading capacity. This protocol provides a versatile, nonviral platform for efficient nucleic acid delivery, supporting applications such as gene-editing experiments.

raw.abstractText: Radiation-induced crosslinking enables the fabrication of protein-based hydrogels and nanogels with tunable physicochemical properties without requiring chemical crosslinkers. Here, we provide protocols for the preparation of protein-based hydrogels that mimic the in vivo extracellular matrix and protein-based nanogels designed for nanomedicine applications, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) contrast agents and drug delivery systems (DDS). The method is based on ionizing radiation of aqueous protein solutions, where hydroxyl radicals generated by water radiolysis react primarily with aromatic amino acid residues (tyrosine, phenylalanine, and histidine), inducing intermolecular crosslinking. The resulting hydrogels and nanogels retain biocompatibility and enzymatic degradability while preserving key cell-adhesive sequences. Bulk hydrogels allow precise control over stiffness and surface topography, whereas nanogels offer size control and support straightforward functionalization. Representative applications include culturing various cell types, such as epithelial, fibroblast, muscle, and stem cell types, on hydrogels with tunable mechanical and topographic cues, and functionalizing nanogels for imaging and therapeutic use. This chapter focuses on gelatin-based hydrogels and nanogels. Supplementary notes direct readers to related protocols for collagen hydrogels and peptide-based nanogels. Collectively, these methods provide a versatile platform for biomaterials and nanomedicine research.

raw.abstractText:
Background

Liver fibrosis is a chronic wound healing process of liver injury and gut-liver axis dysregulation has been recently identified as an important contributor to liver fibrosis progression. Quercetin has been reported to have anti-inflammatory activity and microbiota-modulating effects. However, the potential targets of quercetin remain unclear, as does the relationship between quercetin-associated targets and changes in the gut microbiota in liver fibrosis.

Objectives

The purpose of this study was to use network pharmacology to predict potential targets of quercetin associated with liver fibrosis and to explore changes in gut microbiota following treatment with quercetin using a CCl4-induced rat model.

Methods

Eighteen male Sprague-Dawley rats were randomized into CON group, MOD group and QR group (n = 6 per group). Liver fibrosis was induced by weekly subcutaneous injection of carbon tetrachloride (CCl4) for eight weeks. Oral gavage of quercetin (50 mg/kg/day) was performed in QR group. Histopathological changes were assessed by hematoxylin-eosin staining, Masson staining and Ishak scoring. Potential targets of quercetin were screened using network pharmacology, followed by protein-protein interaction (PPI) network construction and Gene Ontology (GO)/Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses. Cecal microbiota composition was determined by 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Parametric or non-parametric tests were used accordingly, including one-way ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis test.

Results

Histopathology revealed significant liver injury and fibrosis in the MOD group relative to the CON group. The QR group showed lower Ishak fibrosis scores and milder histopathological features compared with the MOD group. Network pharmacology analysis identified UBC, UBE2I, RBX1, PSMB7 and UBA1 as hub targets, with KEGG pathways of interest including the TNF signaling pathway, p53 signaling pathway, Toll-like receptor signaling pathway and ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis. Alpha diversity of the cecal microbiota differed significantly among groups, whereas beta diversity did not. Relative abundance of Proteobacteria decreased and Firmicutes increased in the QR group relative to the MOD group. Taxa enrichment analysis identified enrichment of Muribaculaceae and Ligilactobacillus in the QR group.

Conclusion

Histopathology and microbiome analyses indicated that quercetin intervention was associated with altered liver histopathological features and shifts in gut microbiota composition in rats with CCl4-induced liver fibrosis. Network pharmacology predicted several hub targets and pathways potentially linked to these observations. As the present analyses are purely correlational and lack mechanistic validation at the molecular level, no causal relationships are implied between the predicted targets/pathways and the observed histological or microbiome changes. These findings should be regarded as hypothesis-generating and warrant further validation studies.

raw.abstractText:
Background

Ulcerative colitis is a relapsing inflammatory bowel disease driven by dysregulated immunity, epithelial barrier injury and microbial imbalance. Current therapies remain limited by relapse, adverse effects and incomplete response. Quercetin has anti-inflammatory and barrier-protective activities and ERK-MMP signaling may link inflammation to mucosal tissue damage.

Objectives

To evaluate whether the protective effects of quercetin in experimental ulcerative colitis (UC) are associated with modulation of ERK-MMP signaling, while avoiding causal overinterpretation beyond the animal and cellular evidence.

Methods

A dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced mouse model and a lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophage inflammatory model were used. Mice were allocated to the control, UC model and low-, medium- and high-dose quercetin groups. Disease activity index (DAI; unitless), colon length, histopathology, inflammatory cytokines and ERK/MMP-related molecules were evaluated by histological staining, ELISA, qRT-PCR and western blotting. In-vitro, quercetin was compared with the ERK phosphorylation inhibitor U0126 and an agonistic stimulus to explore pathway-related associations. The study was exploratory and did not include genetic rescue experiments or human validation.

Results

In DSS-treated mice, medium- and high-dose quercetin were associated with improved colon morphology, reduced DAI scores and partial restoration of colon length. Quercetin decreased pro-inflammatory cytokine expression and increased IL-10 expression. In both mouse colon tissues and LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 cells, quercetin was associated with reduced ERK1/2 activation and lower MMP-3 and MMP-9 expression, together with partial recovery of TIMP expression. These molecular changes were directionally consistent with the effects observed after ERK inhibition in-vitro.

Conclusion

Quercetin showed protective effects in experimental UC models and these effects may be associated with modulation of the ERK-MMP signaling axis. Further pathway-specific rescue experiments, pharmacokinetic studies and human-relevant models are required before this mechanism can be considered definitive or clinically translatable.

raw.abstractText: Wilson's disease (WD) is a genetic disorder caused by a mutation in the gene ATP7B. It results in the pathological deposition of copper mainly in the liver and the brain leading to hepatic and neurological manifestations. Medical management is effective in most patients (approximately 85%). It includes chelators (D-penicillamine and trientine), which are the mainstay of treatment, and zinc salts, which are used to inhibit the gastrointestinal absorption of copper. However, in cases of WD with neurological manifestations, patients take longer time to improve and sometimes have persistent clinical symptoms, and a few develop irreversible neurological damage despite adequate chelation. Generally, liver transplantation (LT) is indicated in acute fulminant hepatic failure or decompensated liver cirrhosis (despite adequate chelation). However, LT is still debatable for severe neurologic WD because of advanced or irreversible brain damage. There is a dearth of literature on the role of LT in neurological WD. This study aims to review the current literature concerning indications, contraindications, and outcomes of liver transplantation among children with neurological WD.

raw.abstractText:
Background

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a complex neurodevelopmental condition frequently associated with gastrointestinal (GI) disturbances and alterations in gut microbiota composition. Increasing evidence suggests that the microbiota-gut-brain axis may play a role in the pathophysiology of ASD, raising interest in microbiome-targeted therapies, including probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics, and fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT). However, the clinical effectiveness and mechanisms of these interventions remain incompletely understood due to heterogeneous study designs and variable outcomes across trials.

Aim

To systematically evaluate the clinical efficacy and mechanistic implications of psychobiotic interventions, including probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics, and FMT, in children with ASD.

Methods

We conducted this systematic review in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines. We also followed the methodological recommendations of the Cochrane Handbook. We searched different electronic databases, including PubMed/MEDLINE, EMBASE, Web of Science, PsycINFO, CENTRAL, and CINAHL, from inception till February 2026. We included eligible randomized controlled trials, controlled clinical trials, cohort studies, and pre-post intervention studies evaluating psychobiotic therapies in children and adolescents (≤ 18 years) with ASD. The main outcomes were: (1) Changes in severity as assessed by a broad-spectrum measure of ASD symptomatology at the 3-month follow-up; and (2) Variation of core symptoms, based on validated behavioral scales, including the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule, the Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS), and the Social Responsiveness Scale (SRS). We measured the severity of GI symptoms, microbiome composition, biologicals, and safety as secondary outcomes. Risk of bias was determined with Risk of Bias tool version 2 and Risk of Bias in Non-randomized Studies of Interventions tools. Meta-analysis using random-effects models was conducted where appropriate.

Results

We reviewed 35 clinical studies that examined microbiome-targeted therapies in children with ASD. Overall, probiotics were associated with obvious improvements in GI symptoms and smaller, but noticeable, improvements in behavioral outcomes, although the benefits varied depending on the probiotic strains used, treatment duration, and whether children had GI problems at baseline. When data from selected probiotic studies were pooled, a moderate-to-large overall benefit was observed for GI symptom severity. Prebiotic supplementation mainly benefited gut function and microbial metabolic activity, with little and inconsistent impact on core autism symptoms. Synbiotic approaches-which combine probiotics with fermentable substrates-produced broader effects on the gut microbiome and were linked to modest improvements in both GI and behavioral symptoms. We observed that FMT showed the strongest overall effects among all microbiome-based interventions. Using quantitative analyses, we observed marked improvements in GI symptoms (GI SRS pooled SMD -2.71), along with a significant decrease in key behavioral measures, including social responsiveness (SRS pooled SMD -4.06), aberrant behavior (Aberrant Behavior Checklist -3.00), and overall autism severity (CARS -1.60). However, the strength of this evidence is tempered by the fact that many FMT studies were open-label or non-randomized, which limits confidence in the robustness of these findings. Across all microbiome-targeted therapies, benefits were most consistently observed for GI outcomes, whereas improvements in core ASD symptoms were more variable and less predictable.

Conclusion

Microbiome-targeted therapies are a promising adjunctive strategy in managing children with ASD, especially for associated GI disorders. Probiotics and prebiotics provided the most reliable benefits for GI symptoms, while synbiotics may offer broader microbiome modulation, and FMT has the greatest observed improvements in both GI and behavioral outcomes. However, considerable heterogeneity across studies and limited high-quality randomized trials highlight the need for large, well-designed clinical trials with standardized intervention protocols to clarify clinical efficacy and guide future therapeutic recommendations.

raw.abstractText: Few direct-acting antiviral regimens are approved in China for children and adolescents with chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection and data are limited on their efficacy and safety in this population. This retrospective, multi-centre study aimed to assess the real-world effectiveness and safety of ledipasvir/sofosbuvir (LDV/SOF) and sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (SOF/VEL) in Chinese paediatric patients. The study included patients aged 3-17 years from five hospitals across China who received either LDV/SOF or SOF/VEL for chronic HCV infection. The outcomes included the proportion of patients who achieved sustained virologic response at 12 weeks post-treatment (SVR12), normalisation rates of ALT and AST levels, and incidence of adverse events (AEs). A total of 129 patients from five sites were included and 128 completed 12 weeks of post-treatment follow-up. Mean age was 9.9 years (standard deviation, 3.9), with 30 (23.3%), 55 (42.6%), and 44 (34.1%) patients aged 3-6, 7-11, and 12-17 years, respectively, 84 (65.1%) were male, 62 (48.1%) were infected with genotype 3, and baseline ALT and AST levels were elevated in 64 (49.6%) and 75 (58.1%) patients, respectively. The SVR12 rate was 98.4% (126/128) in the overall population, remaining consistent across subgroups by sex, age, HCV genotype, or regimen. ALT and AST levels were normalised in all patients with available data. AEs were reported by 16.4% (21/128) of patients and none were serious. Collectively, this study demonstrated that LDV/SOF and SOF/VEL were highly effective and well tolerated in Chinese paediatric patients with chronic HCV infection.

Background

Cannabis use may cause psychotic symptoms, such as hallucinations and delusions, as well as persistent amotivation with reduced motivation, inactivity, and cognitive impairment. Although described as cannabis-related amotivational syndrome, it is not recognized as an independent diagnostic entity and overlaps clinically with the negative symptoms of schizophrenia and mood disorders. We report a case of persistent amotivation following cannabis-related psychosis that improved after electroconvulsive therapy (ECT).

Case

A 19-year-old man developed auditory hallucinations, persecutory delusions, and agitation associated with cannabis use and was admitted to a psychiatric hospital. Antipsychotic treatment improved the psychotic symptoms, but marked amotivation and inactivity, accompanied by low performance on cognitive screening, and significantly impaired daily functioning. Depressed mood and appetite loss were not evident. Although negative symptoms of schizophrenia remained a differential diagnosis, the presentation was consistent with cannabis-related amotivational syndrome. Amantadine produced limited improvement. Following ECT, the Apathy Scale score improved from 24 to 7 and the Mini-Mental State Examination score increased from 19 to 26, with improvements in motivation, activity, and daily functioning.

Discussion

This case demonstrates that clinically significant amotivation may persist after cannabis-related psychotic symptoms improve. Persistently reduced motivation and inactivity should not be assumed to represent primary negative symptoms of schizophrenia; rather, clinicians should carefully consider mood symptoms and cannabis-related amotivation in the differential diagnosis. This case also suggests that ECT may represent a treatment option for severe, persistent amotivation following cannabis-related psychosis. However, because this was a single case, further validation through additional cases and long-term follow-up is required.

Background

Insomnia disorder affects approximately 10% of people. The persistence of insomnia, despite treatment, remains high. Cannabis-based medicinal products (CBMPs) have been proposed as a potential treatment for insomnia. This study aims to use data from the UK Medical Cannabis Registry to analyze changes in self-reported sleep quality in patients prescribed CBMPs for insomnia.

Methods

A prospective cohort study of patients treated with CBMPs for insomnia was completed. The primary outcome was the Single-Item Sleep Quality Scale (SQS). This was assessed at baseline and at 1, 3, 6, 12, 18, and 24 months from baseline. Secondary outcomes included change in anxiety and general health-related quality of life. p-values < 0.050 were considered statistically significant.

Results

Two hundred and eleven participants met the inclusion criteria. Over half (n = 126; 59.72%) were users of cannabis at baseline. At the primary endpoint of 24 months, mean SQS improved from 2.46 ± 2.10 (mean ± standard deviation (SD)) at baseline to 5.14 ± 2.75 (mean difference +2.68; 95% confidence interval (CI) 2.23-3.14; p < 0.001), with improvements observed at all timepoints. SQS values of 0 (odds ratio (OR) 15.49; 95% CI 3.87-65.19; p < 0.001) and 1-3 (OR 4.90; 95% CI 1.87-13.80; p = 0.002) at baseline and prescription of dried flower CBMPs (OR 4.99; 95% CI 1.27-21.39; p = 0.025) were associated with clinically significant improvements in sleep quality at 24 months. Seventeen participants (8.06%) reported adverse events. Participants aged over 60 were more likely to report an adverse event (OR 19.08; 95% CI 1.52-535.75; p = 0.036).

Conclusion

Initiation of CBMPs was associated with improvements in self-reported sleep quality across 2 years, with the largest associations observed in those with the most severe impairment. raw.abstractText: The therapeutic effects of antipsychotic drugs are primarily achieved through dopamine D2 receptor antagonism. However, excessive striatal D2 receptor blockade is associated with extrapyramidal side effects (EPS) in schizophrenic patients. Importantly, haloperidol-induced catalepsy was significantly attenuated by scopolamine. Background

Breast cancer (BC) remains a significant global health threat with complex pathogenesis often linked to chemotherapy resistance and inflammatory microenvironments. Histidine triad nucleotide-binding protein 2 (HINT2) is a mitochondrial protein involved in metabolism and immunity, but its specific role in BC and potential as a therapeutic target require further elucidation.

Objectives

This study aimed to identify novel therapeutic targets for BC and evaluate the anti-tumor efficacy and molecular mechanisms of Albiflorin (Al), a natural monoterpene glycoside.

Proteomic profiling was performed on BC xenografts in nude mice to identify differentially expressed proteins. In-vivo and in-vitro models (MDA-MB-231 cells) were established to assess the effects of Al (20 mg/kg or 20 µM) on tumor growth, apoptosis and cytokine production. Furthermore, Al treatment downregulated the HINT2/NLRP3 axis, reduced inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and promoted apoptosis by modulating Caspase-3, Bax and Bcl-2 levels.

Conclusion

Albiflorin suppresses BC progression by inhibiting the HINT2/NLRP3 signaling pathway, suggesting HINT2 is a viable biomarker and Al a promising therapeutic agent for BC treatment.

Background and aims

Hormonal agents and their association with liver injury remain a concern in clinical practice. This study aimed to characterise the biochemical and clinical features of hormonal agent-associated liver injury and compare them with a control group of age- and gender-matched cases of liver injury caused by non-hormonal drugs.

Methods

Of 2123 adjudicated drug-induced liver injury cases enrolled in the Drug-Induced Liver Injury Network (2004-2024), 20 high-confidence cases (1.3%) were attributed to hormonal agents. These cases were compared with age- and sex-matched non-hormonal drug-induced liver injury (DILI) controls, and analyses assessed clinical features, biochemical patterns, outcomes, HLA alleles and candidate genetic variants associated with cholestatic liver disease.

Results

The median age of women was 22 years. Most presented within 2-12 weeks with jaundice and pruritus, predominantly with cholestatic or mixed patterns of liver enzyme elevations, but a hepatocellular pattern was not uncommon at 28%. The route of administration did not appear to influence DILI risk. Half underwent a liver biopsy, and half required hospitalization, but none died or required liver transplantation. Compared with other DILI cases, hormonal agent-associated liver injury was more often cholestatic, with jaundice and pruritus, and less frequently associated with fever or rash. No HLA association was identified, although the intronic MROH2A variant rs6722064 ranked as the top potential candidate for increased risk [OR (95% CI) = 3.58 (1.67, 7.65), p = 0.001].

Conclusions

Hormonal agent-associated liver injury presents with a distinctive mixed or cholestatic pattern and often lacks the inflammatory features seen in other DILI cases. These findings underscore the need for greater clinical awareness to improve patient outcomes.

Background and aims

Liver disease is a significant risk for people who inject drugs due to the high burden of hepatitis C virus (HCV). There is limited data on the impact of the direct-acting antiviral (DAA) therapy era on liver disease among people who inject drugs. This study evaluated baseline and longitudinal liver disease in a national cohort of people who inject drugs recruited over three Waves: 2018-2019, 2019-2021, and 2023-2025.

Methods

The ETHOS Engage Study is an observational cohort of people who inject drugs attending drug treatment clinics and needle and syringe programs in Australia. Participants completed a questionnaire and underwent point-of-care HCV RNA testing (Xpert HCV Viral Load Fingerstick) and liver stiffness measurement (LSM) by vibration-controlled transient hepatic elastography (FibroScan). Advanced chronic liver disease was defined by LSM of 10 kPa or above.

Results

Among all enrolments with a valid LSM (n = 3126, 79% recruited at drug treatment clinics), 11% had advanced chronic liver disease, decreasing from 12.0% (154/1287) in 2018-2019 to 7.9% (66/839) in 2019-2021, and 6.4% (62/967) in 2023-2025. In adjusted analyses, participants recruited between 2019-2021 and 2023-2025 were less likely to have advanced chronic liver disease (vs. 2018-2019; aOR 0.66, 95% CI: 0.48-0.90 and aOR 0.56, 95% CI: 0.40-0.77, respectively). Current HCV infection declined from 24% in 2018-2019 to 10% in 2023-2025. Among participants with LSM in more than one wave and current HCV infection at first visit and no current HCV infection at second visit (n = 44), advanced chronic liver disease declined from 19% to 5%.

Conclusions

Unrestricted access to DAA therapies in Australia has been associated with reduced liver disease burden among people who inject drugs. Monitoring of liver health in this population is important, given potential ageing and non-HCV liver disease impacts.

Aim

To analyse the use of opioids in children with cancer and the experiences of their family members regarding opioids used in pain management to improve family nursing.

Design

An integrative review.

Methods

A systematic literature search was carried out in four databases (CINAHL, MEDLINE, PsycInfo and Scopus) in August 2023, and was subsequently updated to include studies up to the end of 2024. Sixteen peer-reviewed research articles met the inclusion criteria and were included in a quality appraisal and analysis.

Results

Of the wide range of opioids used to treat pain in children with cancer, morphine and fentanyl stood out as the most used. The prevalent routes of opioid administration was intravenous and enteral. Limited research has been conducted on the experiences of family members of children with cancer in the context of opioids used for pain management. Furthermore, there is a scarcity of studies that describe the experiences of siblings from the same perspective. Parental experiences were particularly described as concerns about and a desire to refuse opioid use, although satisfaction with opioid use was also described.

Conclusions

Opioids are particularly significant in managing pain among children with cancer. Therefore, the use of opioids in this patient group should be comprehensively studied, and healthcare professionals should receive sufficient training. The experiences of parents conclude that they require sufficient information and guidance on the management of their children's severe pain and the analgesics used to treat it. The notable lack of research regarding the experiences of siblings in connection with the use of opioids for the management of a child's pain addresses the need for further research from these perspectives. More research on experiences during the different phases of cancer treatment is needed. Further research employing qualitative methods will be essential for enhancing family nursing.

Background

Exposure to mercury (Hg) is well-established to induce menstrual cycle disorders and disrupt sex hormone functions. Astragalus species, characterized by their potent antioxidant and anti-apoptotic properties, have shown potential in mitigating these adverse effects by promoting folliculogenesis and restoring hormonal balance.

Objectives

This study aimed to evaluate the protective effects of Astragalus microcephalus polysaccharides (APS), both alone and in combination with vitamin E and selenium (Vit E+Se), against ovarian damage and oxidative stress induced by mercuric chloride toxicity in rats.

Methods

Thirty-six female Wistar rats were synchronized via vaginal smear and randomly assigned to six groups: Control, Mercury (0.43 mg/kg HgCl2), APS (2.7 g/kg), Vit E+Se, Mercury+APS and Mercury+Vit E+Se. Furthermore, immunohistochemical analysis revealed a significant reduction in stromal and follicular degeneration and a decrease in apoptotic activity in the ovaries of rats treated with APS.

APS exerts a significant protective effect against mercury-induced ovarian toxicity. This protection is mediated through the attenuation of oxidative stress, inflammation and apoptosis, as evidenced by the modulation of Caspase-3, AIF and NF-κB pathways. raw.abstractText: Background Animal-sector antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance requires laboratories capable of recovering bacterial isolates, identifying organisms, performing and interpreting antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST), retaining isolates and associated metadata, and transmitting standardised isolate-level data. This scoping review mapped publicly available information on Australian veterinary diagnostic laboratory services and assessed their potential contribution to animal-sector AMR surveillance. Public websites, submission forms and test directories were reviewed for laboratory identity, sample-submission pathways, culture and isolate recovery, organism identification, AST, reporting, referral and isolate storage. Australian animal-health sources provided the primary framework, while AURA, WHO and CDC priority lists were used only for contextual One Health comparison. Results After duplicating organisational names, former service labels, network-level duplicates, collection centres and unverified internal facilities were reviewed, 20 veterinary laboratory or service entries were retained. These included private laboratory networks, government laboratories, university diagnostic services and selected specialist animal-health and One Health organisations. Publicly available request forms were identified for 14 of 20 entries, sample collection and transport guidance for 10 entries each, turnaround times for seven, and follow-up arrangements for three. AST or “culture and sensitivity” was mentioned for all 20 entries. However, public sources rarely specified the AST platform, antimicrobial panel, interpretive standard and version, minimum inhibitory concentration or inhibition-zone output, quality-control organisms, isolate-selection rules, isolate archiving or submission of isolate-level surveillance data. Pathogen test menus showed broad animal-health and zoonotic coverage, but detection-only or genus-level listings did not establish species-specific identification, resistance-phenotype detection or surveillance-compatible AST capacity. Conclusions Australia has a distributed veterinary diagnostic network with clear potential to support national AMR surveillance. However, publicly available information is insufficient to verify site-level surveillance readiness or determine whether results are produced using comparable methods. A verified registry of physical testing sites, direct confirmation of culture-to-AST workflows, harmonised AST and reporting standards, and a minimum isolate-level dataset are required before routine veterinary laboratory data can be integrated reliably into coordinated national animal-AMR surveillance.

Catatonic and delirious signs overlap, creating treatment dilemmas when sedation obscures diagnostic assessment. We describe serial assessment and medication decision-making in advanced leptomeningeal melanoma during transition to home hospice.

Inpatient observations, investigations, medication exposures, goals-of-care discussions, and serial Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale (BFCRS) examinations were synthesized.

Results

A man in his late 30s with metastatic melanoma involving the leptomeninges and brain developed fluctuating arousal, inattention, disorientation, mutism, immobility, staring, withdrawal, and waxy flexibility. Transient improvements in movement and speech did not translate into sustained gains in attention, communication, intake, mobility, or function. Lorazepam was subsequently reduced and discontinued when severe agitation emerged. As catatonic signs became less sustained and agitation threatened safety, scheduled haloperidol was introduced, with improvement in evening agitation and no documented extrapyramidal symptoms, oversedation, or QTc prolongation. A supervised oral-medication trial supported discharge planning, although hospice placement remained delayed by insurance barriers.

Significance of results

A lower BFCRS score after lorazepam does not necessarily indicate meaningful clinical response if arousal, attention, and function remain impaired. In advanced cancer, catatonic signs may occur within a broader delirious or toxic-neurologic encephalopathy. Serial assessment should therefore incorporate wakefulness, attention, mobility, communication, and patient- and caregiver-defined goals. Treatment should be guided by the immediate priorities of interaction, safety, or comfort and continually reassessed in light of prognosis and feasibility of home care.

raw.abstractText: Currently there is major research interest in the therapeutic potential of serotonergic psychedelic drugs across a range of neuropsychiatric disorders  1-3 . Such drugs exert psychedelic and neuroplastic effects, both likely linked to therapeutic outcomes, via agonist action at the 5-HT  2A receptor  4-7 . This receptor is assumed to generate downstream intracellular signalling via an interaction with either G  q protein coupling and formation of the second messenger inositol trisphosphate (IP  3 ), or through triggering the effector β-arrestin2. Central to the IP  3 pathway is mobilisation of Ca  2+ stored in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Here, we report the unexpected discovery that the 5-HT  2A receptor also signals via an additional second messenger, nicotinic acid adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NAADP), which mobilises Ca  2+ release from lysosomal stores. This effect was revealed through measurement of changes in cellular NAADP levels, pharmacological inhibition of NAADP and direct biosensor measurement of lysosomal Ca  2+ release and was produced not only by 5-HT but also by a range of psychedelic drugs in a receptor-specific manner. Moreover, genetic ablation of the NAADP pathway reduced markers of both hallucinogenic and neuroplastic effects of psychedelic drug administration in mouse models. These findings reveal the involvement of a novel, therapeutically relevant signalling pathway in psychedelic drug action.

raw.abstractText: Background: Since the introduction of proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (¹H-MRS) in epilepsy research in the 1980s, metabolic MRI has provided unique insights into the neurochemical alterations underlying epilepsy. However, evidence has remained fragmented across imaging modalities, epilepsy syndromes, and clinical applications. We systematically reviewed the literature to define the metabolic phenotype of epilepsy and evaluate the evolving role of metabolic MRI in epilepsy research and clinical practice. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, PubMed and Scopus were systematically searched through April 2026 for original human studies investigating metabolic MRI in epilepsy. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction, and quality assessment. Findings were synthesized through structured qualitative evidence, supported by integrated methodological, scientometric, tabular, and visual analyses. Results: A total of 298 studies were included. Focal epilepsy demonstrated widespread alterations involving N-acetyl aspartate, glutamate, Gamma-aminobutyric acid, choline-containing compounds, myo-inositol, lactate, and other metabolites across epileptogenic and brain networks. Generalized epilepsy was characterized by predominantly bilateral and thalamo-cortical metabolic abnormalities, whereas tumor-associated epilepsy showed distinct metabolic alterations within tumors and the peritumoral zone. Treatment and prognostic studies demonstrated metabolite-specific changes following pharmacological and surgical interventions, and emerging metabolic MRI techniques provided complementary information on bioenergetics, ionic homeostasis, glutamatergic cycling, and metabolic flux. Conclusions: The available evidence supports epilepsy as a disorder of distributed metabolic networks that share a common signature of neuronal dysfunction while exhibiting syndrome-specific alterations in neurotransmission, gliosis, and energy metabolism. Complementary metabolic MRI techniques provide distinct biological information, but their clinical translation will require methodological harmonization and multimodal integration.

Background and purpose

Mitophagy impairment plays a key role in Parkinson's disease (PD) progression. Our previous studies showed that lutein, a carotenoid, alleviates PD by inhibiting neuronal ferroptosis and microglial pro-inflammatory polarization. However, whether lutein regulates mitophagy in PD remains unclear. This study investigates the effects and molecular mechanisms of lutein on mitophagy in PD neuronal cells.

Methods

A PD mouse model was established via intraperitoneal injection of MPTP, and an in vitro PD cell model was constructed using MPP+-induced SH-SY5Y cells. Motor deficits in mice were assessed through behavioral tests; brain tissue pathological changes were observed via HE staining; neuronal damage was evaluated by TH immunohistochemistry; mitochondrial membrane potential and autophagy levels were detected using JC-1 staining, western blot, and transmission electron microscopy, while RT-qPCR and western blot measured the expression of key molecules. ChIP-qPCR was used to examine the binding of ATF3 to the PINK1 promoter.

Results

Lutein treatment significantly alleviated MPTP-induced pathological damage in the brain tissue of PD mice, increased the number of TH-positive neurons, and improved motor deficits in PD mice. Additionally, lutein restored mitochondrial membrane potential in MPP+-induced neuronal cells, upregulated LC3B, PINK1, and Parkin protein expression, and ameliorated mitophagy dysfunction in neuronal cells. Mechanistically, lutein attenuates MPP+-triggered upregulation of ATF3. ATF3 overexpression partially counteracts the regulatory effect of lutein on neuronal mitophagy. Moreover, ATF3 directly binds to the promoter region of PINK1 to negatively modulate its transcription. Knockdown of PINK1 reverses the mitophagy activation and neuroprotective effects induced by ATF3 silencing.

Conclusion

Lutein downregulates ATF3, thereby relieving its repression of the PINK1/Parkin signaling pathway and supporting mitochondrial quality control and mitophagy-associated signaling, which slows PD progression.

Purpose of review

Calcium and magnesium remain incompletely individualized in contemporary dialysis prescriptions despite growing evidence linking their concentrations to cardiovascular outcomes, vascular calcification, mineral metabolism, and mortality. The 2025 Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) Controversies Conference report on chronic kidney disease (CKD)-mineral and bone disorder (MBD) and recent kinetic studies of intradialytic ion fluxes make a focused review of these "forgotten" divalent cations timely.

Recent findings

Intradialytic calcium mass transfer is influenced by patient- and prescription-level factors, and total serum calcium incompletely reflects biologically relevant calcium flux; ionized calcium may decline during dialysis as hemoconcentration increases albumin concentration and alkalosis increases albumin-bound calcium. Small randomized trials show that raising dialysate magnesium improves serum resistance to calcification, but whether higher dialysate magnesium improves clinical outcomes remains unknown. The 2025 KDIGO report retains the 1.25-1.50 mmol/l dialysate calcium range and identifies individualized calcium mass-transfer assessment as a research priority. Dial-Mag, a large pragmatic trial comparing higher versus conventional dialysate magnesium concentrations, is ongoing.

Summary

Recent evidence challenges the assumption that standardized dialysate calcium and magnesium prescriptions are optimal for all patients. Future studies should define patient-specific targets, validate practical methods to assess peridialytic calcium and magnesium levels and intradialytic flux, and determine whether individualized dialysate prescriptions improve clinical outcomes.

raw.abstractText: We present a multimodal dataset from twelve healthy adults (aged 19-30 years, 50% female) who completed a 40-hour ultra-short sleep-wake forced desynchrony protocol which scheduled 2 h 30 min of wakefulness in dim light and 1 h 15 min of sleep in darkness (2:1 wake:sleep ratio), with the protocol ending after the last wake period. This schedule compressed the typical 24-hour day into an ultradian 3 h 45 min cycle to decouple circadian and homeostatic influences on physiology and behaviour. During each wake interval, participants completed repeated assessments of visual psychophysics (chromatic temporal contrast sensitivity), pupillometry with silent-substitution stimuli, ocular structure (optical coherence tomography) and physiology (intraocular pressure), psychomotor vigilance, salivary hormones, and standardised questionnaires, alongside continuous actigraphy, electrocardiography, and recordings of core and peripheral temperature, blood pressure, and interstitial glucose. Two supplementary evening sessions under experimental light exposure and dim-light conditions provide comparison data on circadian phase (salivary melatonin concentration, dim-light melatonin onset). Data collected from one pilot participant and screenings of two excluded candidates are additionally included. This dataset supports reuse for investigating circadian dynamics across multiple domains beyond the retinal-function hypotheses of the original study.

raw.abstractText: Phosphoinositides regulate diverse membrane trafficking and signaling events in eukaryotic cells, yet their transbilayer distribution remains largely unexplored, particularly at host-parasite membrane interfaces. Here, we determined the membrane leaflet localization of phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate (PtdIns(4)P) and phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PtdIns(4,5)P2) in Toxoplasma gondii using quick-freezing freeze-fracture replica labeling combined with phosphoinositide-specific probes. Both phosphoinositides were predominantly localized to the cytoplasmic leaflet of the parasite plasma membrane, whereas only weak labeling was detected in the inner membrane complex. PtdIns(4)P, but not PtdIns(4,5)P2, was additionally detected on intracellular vesicles, while mature micronemes lacked detectable labeling for either phosphoinositide. Surprisingly, both phosphoinositides exhibited nearly symmetric distributions between the two leaflets of the parasitophorous vacuole membrane (PVM), in striking contrast to their asymmetric localization in the parasite plasma membrane. Together with our previous demonstration that phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylethanolamine also lose their transbilayer asymmetry in the PVM, these findings indicate that the PVM undergoes global membrane lipid remodeling that extends from major phospholipids to phosphoinositides. We propose that this extensive lipid reorganization represents a defining structural feature of the apicomplexan PVM and provides a new framework for understanding membrane identity at the host-parasite interface.

Background:

Perimenopause is a transitional stage preceding menopause, characterized by hormonal fluctuations and physiological changes that may increase cardiometabolic risk. Emerging evidence suggests that the gut microbiome may influence these changes through estrogen metabolism and microbial metabolite production. Inulin, a prebiotic fiber that modulates the gut microbiome, may offer a targeted nutritional strategy; however, its effects during perimenopause remain largely unexplored.

Objective:

This proof-of-concept study evaluates the effects of short-term inulin supplementation on gut microbiome composition, microbial metabolites, vascular function, skeletal muscle health, and metabolic flexibility in perimenopausal overweight women or with obesity.

Methods:

We will conduct a randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled crossover trial among 27 women aged 40 to55 years. Participants will receive 10 g/day of inulin and a matched maltodextrin placebo for two 14-day intervention periods separated by a 2 to 4-week washout. We will assess changes in gut and vaginal microbiome composition and functional capacity, stool and plasma microbial metabolites, and circulating markers of estrogen metabolism as primary outcomes. We will also evaluate vascular function, skeletal muscle health and oxidative capacity, and metabolic flexibility as secondary outcomes. Additionally, we will assess physical activity, sleep, dietary intake, perimenopausal symptoms, and intervention feasibility, adherence, acceptability, and tolerability.

Conclusion:

This study will provide novel insights into the feasibility and biological effects of inulin supplementation on gut-host mechanisms and cardiometabolic health during perimenopause, informing the design of future larger-scale trials.

Drug and chemical-induced reproductive toxicity encompass diverse disturbances that can impair cellular homeostasis, endocrine function, gametogenesis, and reproductive tissue integrity. Salidroside (Sal), the principal active component of Rhodiola rosea L., exhibits antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective properties; however, its mechanisms of action in AD remain unclear. Sal increased the expression of GSH metabolism-related enzymes, upregulated glutamate-cysteine ligase catalytic subunit and glutamate-cysteine ligase modifier subunit, reduced Keap1 expression, and promoted nuclear Nrf2 accumulation. These effects were associated with alterations in hippocampal GSH metabolism and Keap1/Nrf2/GSH axis activation.

raw.abstractText: Background Smoking is one of the most important modifiable risk factors for lung cancer. However, clinical evidence remains limited regarding whether smoking is associated with remodeling of the lower-airway microbiome and local metabolic networks in patients with lung cancer. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) may reflect the local lower-airway microenvironment, and integrated microbiome-metabolome profiling may help identify smoking-associated ecological and metabolic signatures. Methods Thirty-seven patients with pathologically confirmed lung cancer who underwent electronic bronchoscopy at the Second Hospital of Hebei Medical University between November 2022 and November 2023 were enrolled, including 22 smokers and 15 never-smokers. BALF samples were collected for 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and untargeted metabolomic profiling. Smoking-associated microbial taxa, metabolites, and cross-omics associations were evaluated using LEfSe, KEGG enrichment, ROC curve analysis, and Spearman correlation analysis. Results A total of 1,378 operational taxonomic units were detected, including 1,004 shared OTUs. Alpha diversity did not differ significantly between groups, whereas weighted UniFrac PCoA showed significant separation in microbial community structure (PERMANOVA, P < 0.05). Bacteroidota, Actinomycetota, Prevotella, Schaalia, and Mobiluncus were relatively enriched in smokers, whereas Pseudomonadota, Finegoldia, Peptoniphilus, and Paracoccus were enriched in never-smokers. Untargeted metabolomics identified 23 differential metabolites, of which 18 were upregulated and 5 were downregulated in smokers. These metabolites were mainly enriched in glutathione metabolism, alanine metabolism, arginine and proline metabolism, bile secretion, ABC transporters, pantothenate and coenzyme A biosynthesis, and fructose and mannose metabolism. ROC analysis suggested potential discriminatory value for (Z)-11-hexadecenal, spermidine, oxosativene, nicotine N-oxide, and 1,2-dimethylimidazole (AUC 0.706–0.776). Mobiluncus was positively correlated with nicotine N-oxide, whereas Finegoldia was negatively correlated with dihydrothymine. Conclusions BALF from smokers with lung cancer showed local microenvironmental alterations characterized by microbial compositional remodeling and metabolic pathway perturbation. The observed Mobiluncus-nicotine N-oxide and Finegoldia-dihydrothymine associations are candidate microbiome-metabolome features that require validation in larger, well-matched cohorts.

raw.abstractText: Long-term exposure to paraquat (PQ), a widely used herbicide, has been linked to increased risk of Parkinsons Disease (PD) in agricultural workers and rural communities in the United States (US), findings further supported by experimental animal studies. Although banned in many countries across the globe, PQ remains widely used in the US. Inhalation of PQ has been known to induce systemic organ failure at acute concentrations. However, prolonged low-dose inhalation from agricultural spraying and pesticide drift has not been readily evaluated for its potential to contribute to neurodegenerative diseases in vivo. Instead, many experimental studies have relied on systemic routes of exposure, which do not effectively replicate the most common route of exposure to PQ in the environment. In the current study, Parkinsonian features were examined in mice that had been exposed via whole-body inhalation to PQ aerosol for either 40 or 60 days. Levels of PQ in brain were highest in olfactory bulb, followed by frontal cortex and then brainstem in both sexes. After 60 days of exposure, male-specific impairments in locomotor activity were observed, in addition to reductions in striatal dopamine, in substantia nigra tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression and number of TH+ dopaminergic neurons, the latter being considered the primary basis of PD, along with increased olfactory bulb α-synuclein levels. As such, these studies confirm the dopaminergic neurotoxicity of inhaled PQ. These findings raise significant concerns as to the contribution of PQ exposures to the continued increase in the incidence of PD in the US.
